# Interview Preparation Guide

## STAR Format

Structure answers as: **Situation** (context), **Task** (your responsibility), **Action** (what you did), **Result** (outcome).

Keep answers to 1-2 minutes. Be specific. End with what you learned or would do differently.

## Ready-Made STAR Examples

## STAR Candidates (Complete Manually)

### GE Vernova I/O Subsystem + Serial Modbus (Firmware from Scratch)
**S:** Our industrial radios had been shipping with IO pins physically wired on the PCB but no firmware logic behind them — customers couldn't use the IO capability at all. The existing codebase had bare read/write calls for the three pins but nothing user-configurable, nothing persisted across power cycles, and nothing exposed through the CLI. Separately, while TCP Modbus was technically enabled in the codebase, there was no data dictionary — no mapping of Modbus addresses to actual device data — so it was completely non-functional in practice. There was also no serial RTU or ASCII Modbus support at all.
**T:** Design and implement a complete IO subsystem from scratch — persistent per-pin configuration, hardware-aware setup, PWM output, ADC input, interrupt-driven edge counting, CLI commands, and a config dictionary — plus add serial Modbus RTU and ASCII drivers with a full register dictionary, all targeting an OTA firmware update that would ship to every unit already in the field.
**A:** Designed an NVS-backed configuration system so IO mode assignments (digital in, digital out, analog in, PWM out) survive power cycles. Reverse-engineered the PCB's FET-based dual-pin IO architecture — each port uses separate dout and din pins with FETs to switch the power rail, requiring dout to be held high before din can be enabled — and wrote hardware setup functions that enforce these constraints correctly. Implemented PWM output via STM32 timers, ADC sampling for the analog input port, and interrupt-driven edge counting (configurable for rising, falling, or both edges). Added CLI commands and dictionary entries so end users can configure each pin's mode through the existing user interface. In parallel, wrote serial Modbus RTU and ASCII drivers from scratch, researched and identified which data points were worth exposing (signal strength, device temp, IO states, uptime, alarm statuses, and ~100 others), and built the Modbus address dictionary that maps register addresses to that live device data — making both the new serial Modbus and the previously-useless TCP Modbus functional for the first time.
**R:** Pending OTA release. Once shipped, every existing unit in the field will receive IO capability retroactively — customers can configure door-open counters, temperature reads, and other station monitoring without adding external hardware. The serial Modbus addition enables remote real-time monitoring of signal strength, device temperature, IO states, uptime, and alarm statuses without requiring on-site access or SSH, giving network operators a live view of device health across an entire deployment.
**Use for:** "Tell me about a time you built something complex from scratch", "How do you approach a new firmware feature on unfamiliar hardware?", "Describe a project where you had to understand the hardware before you could write the firmware", "Tell me about something you shipped that had real user impact"

### Lockheed Martin QA Automation Tool (75% Reduction in Review Time)
**S:** The QA team had two engineers supporting 35 developers. Every PR required a manual review against a checklist — hardcoded values, variable naming conventions, dependency versions, coding format compliance, README completeness, proof-of-work screenshots, and a valid linked Jira ticket — taking 20–35 minutes per review. With the volume of PRs from 35 developers, the team was struggling to keep up.
**T:** Collaborated with one other intern (Travis did the majority of the implementation) to build a Python tool that automated as much of the checklist as possible, plus additional checks the QA team flagged informally as useful but hadn't formally documented.
**A:** Implemented regex-based scanning for naming convention violations, forbidden keywords, and format compliance. Built commented-out code detection to catch executable logic hidden in comments. Integrated the GitHub API to verify that every listed dependency actually existed in the expected repo and was pinned to the latest release — not to a `main` branch. Integrated the Jira API to confirm a valid, related ticket was linked in every PR. Added screenshot detection to verify proof-of-work was included. One of the harder problems was the README validator: each developer structured required sections differently (dependency tables, bullet lists, comma-separated inline), so wrote a flexible parser that could recognize the required content regardless of formatting. Gathered feedback from the QA team iteratively throughout development so the tool matched their actual workflow by the time it shipped.
**R:** Review time dropped from 20–35 minutes to 5–10 minutes (75% reduction at lower bounds). Over 60% of checklist items were fully automated. The QA team integrated the tool into the GitLab CI pipeline as an automated check phase that runs on every PR — developers see the results before QA ever looks at the code, eliminating time wasted reviewing PRs that fail on trivial criteria like a missing title prefix or absent screenshot.
**Use for:** "Tell me about a time you improved a process", "Give an example of measurable impact you had", "Describe a project where you had to understand someone else's workflow before writing code", "Tell me about a time you worked with a teammate to deliver something"

### RIT EVT VCU — Real-Time Motorcycle Control System (CANopen + RTOS from Scratch)
**S:** The RIT Electric Vehicle Team's track motorcycle needed a full vehicle control unit to coordinate the motor controller, power subsystem, battery management system, and accessory network. The existing VCU firmware was roughly 100 lines — a simple state machine that toggled power to components and issued rider warnings. It had no communication stack, no real-time control loop, and no integration with the team's new custom PCB designed by the EEs.
**T:** Build the VCU firmware nearly from scratch as the sole firmware engineer (95% solo, occasional support from others), coordinating with electrical engineers who designed the custom STM32F446 PCB and produced a Simulink-generated 300 Hz state machine that needed to run under hard real-time constraints.
**A:** Learned CAN and CANopen from zero — came in knowing only that CAN was a differential signal — and built the full CANopen object dictionary from scratch, defining PDO mappings for asynchronous data exchange with the motor controller, battery management system, and power subsystem across dual CAN buses (powertrain and accessory networks). Set up timing, heartbeat, and sync, and added support for software-triggered CANopen message sending. Integrated the Simulink-generated state machine into ThreadX RTOS and hit an immediate hard timing problem: the state machine couldn't hit 300 Hz at the STM32's default clock configuration. Diagnosed the bottleneck and resolved it by overclocking the STM32 to a higher-than-default but within-spec clock rate to meet the deadline. Built board-level fault handling, drive-by-wire control, and system health monitoring on top of the communication stack.
**R:** VCU firmware complete. First powered test had been delayed by a battery hardware issue (not firmware) — that's since been resolved, and the bike successfully ran with the VCU for the first time in late September 2026. The team typically competes in approximately two races per motorcycle per year. Note for interviews: this is now a finished, working result, not just "firmware done, testing pending" — lead with the successful run.

**Functional safety note (added 2026-10-07):** The VCU's design is informed by ISO 26262 and IEC 61508 concepts, not formally certified to them. Current architecture is a single-channel setup (**1oo1** in IEC 61508 terms) — that's what's running and what had the successful track day. In progress: a second, independent diagnostic microcontroller that monitors the main chip's inputs/outputs/behavior and can force a safe shutdown, which would bring it to a full **1oo1D** architecture. That diagnostic chip isn't built yet — be accurate about tense: 1oo1 is done, 1oo1D is in progress. The planned fault-recovery behavior requires an explicit key-cycle before the bike can resume, rather than silently recovering from a fault. Good material for any safety-critical-systems conversation (automotive, aerospace, defense), not just one specific company.
**Use for:** "Tell me about a time you had to learn something completely new under pressure", "Describe a hard real-time constraint and how you met it", "How do you approach firmware on hardware someone else designed?", "Tell me about a complex system you built as the primary engineer", "What's the most technically challenging project you've worked on?", "Do you have any experience with functional safety or safety-critical design?"

### GE Vernova Web Dashboard Memory Leak (Systematic Debugging)
**S:** Built a web dashboard as a side project at GE to monitor the radio network. Left it running over a weekend and came in Monday to find the browser had crashed — the app was leaking memory and couldn't sustain continuous runtime, which made it useless as a monitoring tool.
**T:** Diagnose and fix the leak so the dashboard could run indefinitely without crashing.
**A:** On Monday morning, restarted the dashboard and immediately captured a Firefox memory report as a baseline. Left it running overnight and captured a second report Tuesday morning. Comparing the two reports revealed DOM and JavaScript leaks growing over time. Spent a couple of days tracing and fixing the issues, using AI tooling to help isolate the specific leak sources. Found the root cause was a combination of things — including the underlying Python library itself contributing to the leaks. Swapped the library out for Flask, which eliminated the remaining issues.
**R:** Achieved stable multi-day continuous runtime with no crashes. The dashboard became a reliable monitoring tool for the radio network. Note for interviews: if asked about AI assistance in debugging, be straightforward — used it as a tool to help isolate root causes faster, same way you'd use a Stack Overflow search or a colleague's input.
**Use for:** "Tell me about a difficult bug you tracked down", "How do you approach debugging a non-obvious issue?", "Describe a time your work improved system reliability", "How do you use available tools and resources when you're stuck?"

### Autonomous Fixed-Wing Flight Controller (Sensor Fusion + Autonomous Control — In Progress)
**S:** Wanted to build a fully autonomous fixed-wing RC drone from scratch — not just fly one, but design the flight controller hardware and write all the firmware personally. No prior experience with flight control, PID, or sensor fusion algorithms. The core challenge is that autonomous fixed-wing flight is fundamentally harder than multirotor: a fixed-wing can't hover, requires coordinated control surfaces to turn, and has no margin for a poorly-tuned control loop at speed.
**T:** Design and build a custom flight controller on an ESP32S3 that supports RC passthrough, PID-based stabilization, and eventually full autonomous GPS waypoint navigation — all written from scratch in C.
**A:** Designed and fabricated a custom PCB (v1 complete, v2 in progress). Wrote GPS and IMU drivers from scratch. Integrated the Madgwick IMU/AHRS sensor fusion algorithm — the library was C++ but the rest of the codebase is C, so wrote a C wrapper to bridge them cleanly. Built PWM input and output drivers around ESP-IDF's MCPWM library for reading RC receiver signals and driving servos/motor. Implemented RC passthrough mode (direct input-to-output) and a hardware switch that toggles into autonomous mode. Set up background threads that continuously update global GPS and IMU state. Implemented PID loops for roll and pitch stabilization — first time working with PID — and is currently working through how to combine control loops for coordinated turns, which requires understanding the coupling between aileron, elevator, and rudder inputs. Roadmap: tune and flight-test the stabilization PID, then add GPS waypoint following, then automatic takeoff and landing, with a stretch goal of two-drone formation flying with inter-aircraft coordination.
**R:** In progress, but with real flight data now. First test flight happened October 3, 2026, manual mode (RC passthrough) only — autonomous PID stabilization hasn't been flight-tested yet. The flight surfaced an RF issue (signal dropping, some mishaps), currently being debugged before the next round of testing. Sensor fusion (Madgwick AHRS), GPS tracking, and PID stabilization loops are implemented and SITL-validated (80-scenario regression suite), but not yet proven in the air. Note for interviews: this is honest, positive progress — "we flew it, found a real issue, and we're debugging it" is a better story than "still on the bench," don't undersell it just because the RF bug isn't fixed yet.
**Use for:** "What are you building outside of work or school?", "Tell me about a time you had to learn an entirely new domain", "How do you approach a problem where you don't know the answer upfront?", "Tell me about a project that's pushing your limits", "Do you have experience with sensor fusion or control systems?"

### Chip-8 Emulator Console (Deliberate Breadth Project — Six Firsts in One)
**S:** While working full-time, wanted to build something entirely self-made end-to-end — not just write code, but own every layer: the software, the PCB, the physical assembly, and the enclosure. Also wanted a reason to learn Rust. Chose Chip-8 as a deliberately approachable scope so the challenge would come from the breadth of new domains, not the complexity of any single one.
**T:** Build a working handheld Chip-8 emulator console from scratch, personally touching every part of the stack: firmware, PCB design, soldering, display driver, and physical enclosure — mostly working a few hours per week alongside a full-time internship.
**A:** Wrote the Chip-8 emulator in Rust — first time using the language — learning it incrementally over several months. Designed a 4x4 matrix keypad PCB in KiCad — first time doing PCB layout — working through a few YouTube tutorials to get up to speed. Hand-soldered all the components including tiny SMD resistors and diodes, which was a first; the fine-pitch parts were difficult but manageable with patience. Wrote a custom SPI display driver for an SSD1309 OLED on the Raspberry Pi, avoiding external graphics libraries to keep it low-level. Designed a custom enclosure in CAD software and 3D printed it — first time using both a CAD tool and a 3D printer.
**R:** A working handheld Chip-8 console, every part of which was personally designed and built. Six distinct firsts in one project: Rust, PCB design, soldering, SMD components, custom SPI drivers, and 3D-printed enclosure. The project did exactly what it was designed to do — broad exposure to the full hardware-software stack in one self-contained build.
**Use for:** "Tell me about a personal project you're proud of", "How do you approach learning something completely new?", "Describe a time you took initiative outside of work or school", "What do you do to keep growing technically on your own time?"

### GE Vernova — Three Parallel Workstreams (Competing Priorities / Self-Direction)
**S:** While working on Modbus cleanup and MQTT support for the radio (production code, highest implicit priority), Travis's manager brought on two additional workstreams in quick succession. First, a facility solar panel upgrade: connect three Modbus-capable solar controllers on parking lot light posts to radio units so live solar data could be shown to clients during in-person tours — with a seasonal deadline, since heavy snow would make outdoor installation and tours impractical once winter arrived. Second, a customer demo: build a pan/tilt mini solar panel mounted on two servos controlled via the radio's I/O and driven over Modbus, to showcase both I/O and Modbus capabilities to prospective clients. All three overlapped for one to two months, with prioritization largely self-directed.
**T:** Manage all three workstreams simultaneously without explicit task scheduling from the manager — keeping production Modbus/MQTT moving as the top priority, hitting the solar project's implicit seasonal deadline, and making steady background progress on the demo when opportunities arose.
**A:** Kept Modbus/MQTT as the primary daily focus since it was production code. Recognized early that the solar hardware procurement was not blocked by Modbus completion — identified the controllers, wiring, and cables needed, wrote the project proposal, got it approved, and placed the order during Modbus work to absorb the shipping lead time rather than letting it create downtime later. Used natural lulls in the production work to make incremental progress on the demo: sourced a pan/tilt gimbal, designed a physical enclosure, connected two servos to the radio's I/O ports, and wrote a control script that drove both servo positions over Modbus. Kept the demo explicitly deprioritized since it had no deadline, advancing it only when the other two had breathing room.
**R:** Modbus and MQTT support completed for production. Solar panel upgrade fully implemented: three solar controllers installed on facility light posts, each connected to a radio unit, providing wireless real-time solar data used during on-site client tours — completed before the seasonal window closed, total hardware cost approximately $350. Customer demo completed shortly after; pending first showing to clients. Note: the proactive hardware ordering eliminated what would have been a multi-week blocking delay if procurement had waited until Modbus was done.
**Use for:** "Tell me about a time you had to juggle competing priorities", "How do you manage multiple projects at once?", "Tell me about a time you self-directed your work without close oversight", "Tell me about a time you anticipated a problem before it happened"

### GE Vernova — Modbus Briefing (Explaining Technical to Non-Technical)
**S:** After shipping Modbus support and building a web dashboard to interface with it, a salesperson was preparing to present the radio product at an industry convention. They had no embedded or networking background but needed to confidently demo the new capabilities — including features I'd built — to potential buyers.
**T:** Brief the salesperson well enough that they could present and field questions without me in the room, in a way that would actually land with customers rather than confuse or bore them.
**A:** Started by identifying the buzzwords that matter to industrial buyers — "Modbus" itself is an industry-standard protocol that procurement engineers recognize, so naming it correctly was important. Explained the features in terms of customer value rather than implementation: not "we added RTU/ASCII drivers" but "you can now pull live diagnostic data from the radio using any Modbus-compatible tool your customers already have." Flagged three specific things to highlight on the webapp and what each one meant to a buyer: the live Modbus data feed (proof that the radio can expose status and diagnostics over a standard protocol), the RTT display on pings (one of the product's genuine competitive advantages — lower round-trip time than comparable products), and the historical data graph (customers respond to visuals, and it shows performance over time at a glance). Gave concrete field use examples so the salesperson could answer "when would I use this?" naturally. The main technique throughout: relate unfamiliar things to things they already understand — but treat them as a knowledgeable adult who knows customers and markets well. Talking down to someone who understands the business better than you do backfires immediately.
**R:** The salesperson presented at the convention and came back saying it went wonderfully. The briefing gave them enough to demo confidently and explain the value proposition without technical backup.
**Use for:** "Tell me about a time you explained something technical to a non-technical audience", "How do you communicate with people outside your discipline?", "Give an example of cross-functional communication"

## Common Tough Questions

### "Why did you leave Lockheed Martin?"
> "The internship had a defined end date — Lockheed's program is 3 months, and RIT's co-op requirement is 8 months, so returning wasn't logistically possible. But separately, while I learned a lot from the QA work — the rigor, understanding the development process from the quality side — my core passion has always been embedded firmware, and I wanted my next role to be as close to the hardware as possible. No hard feelings toward Lockheed; it was a great experience. It just clarified exactly what kind of work I wanted to do next."
>
> **Follow-up: "Would you go back?"** → "I'd consider it — they do solid work. But I'd want an embedded firmware role, not QA. The 8-month co-op requirement is also a constraint, so it'd depend on what they had available." (Note: this question almost never comes from Lockheed themselves — it's a casual aside at other companies. Honest answer is fine.)
> **Follow-up: "What didn't you like about QA?"** → "QA taught me a lot about rigor and process — I'm glad I did it. My core interest has always been firmware; I wanted to get closer to the hardware."

### "Why are you leaving GE Vernova?"
> "My co-op ends in December, so it's a natural transition point. I'm really proud of what I shipped there — the I/O subsystem, the Modbus stack — and I grew a lot both technically and as a team member. But what I'm most energized by is firmware that controls physical systems: actuators, motor controllers, flight surfaces, powertrain. The work I've done at GE is great, but the application domain is industrial radio networking. I'm specifically targeting my next role in [interviewer's domain] because that's where my heart is — and I want to spend my next internship as close to that as possible."
>
> **Key framing:** This is a positive pull toward their domain, not a complaint about GE. Never say "it wasn't my dream field" — say what you *are* excited about instead.
> **Follow-up: "What didn't you like about GE?"** → Nothing about the company. Love the team, proud of what I shipped. Purely domain preference.
> **Follow-up: "Would you go back?"** → On good terms, but actively pursuing [their domain] specifically.

### "You don't have [specific skill/experience]."
> [PREPARE YOUR ANSWER — acknowledge the gap, bridge to adjacent experience (e.g., different MCU family but same HAL/RTOS patterns), show willingness to learn quickly from datasheets]

### "Where do you see yourself in 5 years?"
> "In five years, I want to be a senior embedded engineer — still hands-on, still writing firmware, still at the bench when something isn't working. I want to have grown to the point where I'm owning larger pieces of a system: not just implementing a subsystem from a spec, but contributing to the design decisions earlier in the process.
>
> The piece that matters to me beyond that is being in a position to work alongside interns. My internships have been the most formative experiences of my career so far — the problems are real, the stakes are real, and you learn faster than anywhere else. I want to eventually be on the other side of that: the engineer who hands an intern a real problem and helps them grow through it. I already do some of this informally on my college EV team, helping onboard new members, and I genuinely enjoy it.
>
> I'm not drawn to a purely management track — I want to stay technical. But a tech lead role where I'm still contributing while also mentoring is something I'd find really rewarding."
>
> **Delivery notes:** Swap "senior embedded engineer" for the company's specific domain when relevant (e.g. "defense firmware engineer" at Raytheon, "flight software engineer" at SpaceX). The internship paragraph is your differentiator — almost no one gives this answer, and it's genuine.

### "What's your biggest weakness?"

Two polished options — pick one per interview depending on context.

**Option A: Polishing non-critical things** (signals: quality-minded, detail-oriented)
> "My biggest weakness is that when I'm working in a codebase and I notice something that could be cleaner — a confusing variable name, a function doing too much, a non-obvious algorithm with no context — I have a hard time leaving it alone, even if it's not what I'm there to fix. I'll add a comment explaining a hardware constraint, or reorganize a file, even when none of it affects runtime behavior or the task I was assigned.
>
> The upside is the code is usually better for it. The downside is it's a real time sink, and sometimes what I 'quickly cleaned up' took 30 minutes I hadn't budgeted. I've gotten better at asking myself: *is this actually improving maintainability, or am I just scratching an itch?* — and if it's the latter, logging a note to come back to it rather than doing it right now. But it's still something I actively have to check myself on."

**Option B: Asking for help too late** (signals: team-aware, self-directed, respectful of others' time)
> "My tendency is to try to solve problems myself before bringing them to someone else — especially a manager. I don't want to interrupt someone for every small thing, so I'll dig through documentation, try different approaches, trace through the hardware. The problem is I sometimes take too long to recognize that what I thought was a small blocker is actually something I genuinely need help with.
>
> To manage it, I set myself a time limit. If I'm still stuck when it's up, or I context-switch to something else and come back still blocked, I don't just walk over and say 'I'm stuck' — I write up everything: what the problem is, what I tried, what I learned, what I still don't understand. That way I'm not making someone reconstruct the context from scratch, and honestly, the act of organizing it clearly often helps me spot what I was missing. But the discipline of actually stopping and asking is something I still have to actively manage."

### "Why this company specifically?"
> Customize per company. Must reference: specific products, embedded domains they work in, tech stack, or team structure. Never give a generic answer.

## Questions You Should Ask Interviewers

### About the Role
- "What does a typical week look like in this role?"
- "What would success look like in the first 6 months?"
- "What's the biggest challenge the team is facing right now?"

### About the Team
- "How big is the team, and how do you divide work?"
- "What does the development/project lifecycle look like, from idea to production?"
- "How do you onboard new team members?"

### About Tech & Growth
- "What's your current embedded stack — MCU families, RTOS, toolchain?"
- "Is there room to grow into more architectural or system-level design decisions?"
- "How does the team stay current with new tools and methods?"

### About Culture (use these to prevent disappointment)
- "How would you describe the team culture?"
- "What does professional development look like here?"
- "Is there flexibility for remote/hybrid work?"
- "What's the balance between new development and maintenance work?"
- "How would you describe the leadership style in this team?"
- "What do people who thrive here have in common?"

## Phone/Video Interview Tips
- Have STAR examples written out (use this file)
- Keep a glass of water nearby
- Smile when speaking (it changes your tone)
- Ask for clarification if a question is vague
- It's OK to take 5 seconds to think before answering
- End with: "Is there anything else you'd like to know about my background?"

## After the Application (Best Practice)

### Follow-Up Etiquette
- **Don't call to "stand out"** or to learn more about the role post-submission — this risks a negative impression
- If the employer specified a timeline, respect it and wait
- If no timeline was given and significant time has passed (2+ weeks), a brief check-in is acceptable
- If you have genuinely new, relevant information to share, a short follow-up is fine

### Thank-You Notes
- When you receive any update (interview invitation, rejection, or status update), send a brief thank-you message
- Express appreciation for their time and the process
- Keep it short (2-3 sentences)

## Roleplay Guidelines
When the user asks for interview practice:
1. Ask which role/company to simulate
2. Start with easy warm-up questions ("Tell me about yourself")
3. Progress to role-specific technical questions (MCU families, protocols, debugging approaches)
4. Include 1-2 behavioral questions using the competencies from the job posting
5. End with a tough question or curveball
6. After each answer, give brief feedback: what worked, what to sharpen
7. Suggest which STAR example would work best for each question
